`go run ./cmd/bench -blocks 32,64,128,256,512,1024 <family>` — the non-default
block list is what every committed `results/*.csv` was measured with, so keep
it if rows are to stay comparable. `go generate ./...` first if any `.comp`
changed (`*.spv` is gitignored). As of 2026-09-13 the `moe` family is ~9
minutes / 896 rows; it prints its summary tables only at the end, so there is
no progress output to poll — run it in the foreground with a long timeout.
The `bank` family (added 2026-09-15, research/llm-vertical.md L0a) is the odd one out: its 72
timed cells are seconds, but `go run ./cmd/bench -bankgib 64 -bankreadmib 1024
bank` first allocates 64 GiB in 19 buffers and writes one word per 4 KB page,
which is most of its ~3-minute wall clock. Check `free -g` has the headroom
before starting it.

**A whole-model tok/s number is only comparable against a control run the
same hour** (P1c, 2026-09-18): with an identical binary the decode step
measured 30.51 ms one day and 39.20 the next — every *dense-bank* kernel
1.6-1.9x slower (dn.qkv 115→206 us, head 1964→3531) while every MoE
expert-bank rung was unchanged. Suspected GTT page fragmentation of the
float-staged dense banks (32-day uptime, swap 100% full); unprovable without
root. **And a difference below ~0.5 tok/s needs interleaved A/B/A/B pairs, not one
pair** (P3, 2026-09-18): three pairs of the same two banks gave −0.06, +0.14
and +0.05 tok/s, so either single pair would have reported a signed number
where the truth was a within-arm spread of 0.31 against a real difference of
~0.04. Quote the means and the within-arm spread, not one delta.

So when measuring a decode/prefill change, rebuild yesterday's code in
a worktree (`.spv` are gitignored — regenerate or copy them) and run both
binaries back to back; never quote a delta against a prior day's CSV. Also:
run 1 of a freshly staged graph diverges from runs 2+ at ~1.6e-5 in the
logits (research/p1c-prerecorded-decode.md finding 4) — warm the graph once
before any bitwise comparison.

One-token `-ladder` runs of `cmd/llm` (moe/dn/attn/hc) must defeat the 32 MiB
MALL or every rate is an L3 number: stage many layers and use `-iters 1`
(e.g. `-moe -tokens 1 -ladder -layers 16 -iters 1`, P1b 2026-09-18 —
`ProfileSweep` walks a dispatch kind across layers, so each timing reads a
cold bank). The screen: any CSV row whose gbps exceeds 242 was not measuring
DRAM. The default two-layer, 20-iter form re-reads a ~32 MB working set from
the MALL.

**`go generate` after a `.comp` edit is load-bearing, and skipping it fails
*silently and flatteringly*.** `.spv` is gitignored and embedded into the Go
binary, so an edited shader that was not regenerated runs the **previous**
kernel — and a hand-compile to `/tmp` to check syntax is not the same thing.
On 2026-09-19 (P5b) that produced a whole round of measurements that read as a
2x speed-up and a full set of green tests, because the old kernel was doing
half the work on the new grid. Regenerate just the families touched
(`grep "go:generate" shaders/shaders.go | grep <file>.comp | sed 's|^//go:generate ||'`
into a loop) and check the `.spv` mtime before believing any number.

**Why:** the repo's TODO.md handoffs report a reproducibility figure for every
session (two runs of the family, median ratio and p10-p90 over common rows),
so a session that measures anything is expected to run its family twice and
quote the agreement.

**How to apply:** budget ~20 minutes for two `moe` runs, save each log and CSV
to the scratchpad so run N-1 survives for the comparison, and check nothing
else is using the GPU (`/sys/class/drm/card1/device/gpu_busy_percent`) before
starting. **"Nothing else" includes your own `go build` and `go test`** — a
whole-model decode step is ~3 ms of host work in ~28, and compiling beside a

**`go test ./llm/` needs `-timeout 60m`.** Go's default is ten minutes and the
suite runs past it inside `TestQSASelectionSurvivesOurScores`. What you get is
a panic stack and `FAIL strix-halo-vulkan/llm 600.024s`, which **reads as a
real failure and is not one**. With a warm bank cache the whole suite is
~180 s; cold it is much longer.

**`TestGraphLogits` passes as of 2026-09-22** — it now takes a near-tie on
argmax (7 tokens, "The capital of France is Paris."). Its diagnostics at
f062e28 are `result_output ... maxAbs 1.987e+00 at 19208, rms 3.314e-01`,
argmax ours 11751 vs llama.cpp 561, "0.4920 apart" — P16's three changes
reproduce them byte for byte. (The older `2.507e+00 at 141557` digits are from
before the test changed.) To get a base to diff against, a `git worktree` of
HEAD needs `models/` and `reference/out/` symlinked in (both gitignored) and
the `.spv` files copied, or the test silently prints nothing.

**That identity is also the cheapest whole-model bit-exactness check there
is.** A change that claims to be bit-exact should reproduce those numbers to
the digit through all 48 layers — stronger than any block test, and it costs
one 61 s run.

**`LLM_BANK_CACHE` is a relative path, and `go test ./llm/` resolves it
against `llm/`.** So exporting the usual
`LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache` and running the
tests silently builds a **23 GB** duplicate at `llm/models/`, untracked. Use
an absolute path, or `rm -rf llm/models` afterwards. The real cache
(26 GB, 199 files) is at the repo root.

**How to apply:** the useful per-change gates are
`go test ./llm/ -run 'TestAttn|TestMoEGPU|TestGraphIsAChunkSplit' -timeout 30m`
(~80 s), and run the full suite only when something broad moved. See

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

new='''**The day:** 26.66 → 25.13 ms a step, **37.5 → 39.8 tok/s** (P19's head,
P21a, P22a, P21c).

## Finding 6 — the moves deleted without a shared arena (P22b): 196 → 4 a step, 25.13 → 24.83

The 196 moves were the largest weightless item above (0.53 ms, 2.7 µs
each), and L6c's answer to them was a shared arena it priced and refused:
splitting every block's `alloc` into a layout pass and a materialisation
through five constructors. **There is another way to delete a copy: bind
the other block's arena in the kernel on either side of the boundary.** A
compute pipeline here owns its descriptor set, so a pipeline can be built
per (kernel, foreign buffer) — which is exactly what `llm_move.comp`
already was, nine pipelines for nine buffer pairs — and binding 11 is that
foreign buffer, 5–10 padded with the bank (`XOUT`/`XIN` in
`llm_common.glsl`, `HCLink` in `gpu.go`, built on first use because the
sublayers' arenas exist only once the graph does).

- **The output side, at every row count.** `llm_hc_cn.comp` and
  `llm_hc_combine.comp` read the block output out of the sublayer's own
  fp32 arena (`xout[outOff + t*n + i]`) — the same floats the move copied.
  The graph holds a combine as before (`pending`) and now remembers where
  the sublayer left its output (`pendingOut`); the PLE flush and the last
  flush read it there too.
- **The input side, on the decode GEMV.** `llm_hc_up_gemv.comp`'s epilogue
  has the mixer's value in a register, so the `XIN` build stores
  `float16_t(s * invHC)` straight into the sublayer's A operand at the
  consumer's stride (two PLE fields carry the stride and the row block, on
  the SEQ_PAST rule) and skips the fp32 `mixed` store. The padded GEMM at
  prefill still writes `mixed` and the graph moves it; `RunLinked` says
  which happened. What is left to the mover at decode is the PLE block's
  wide residual out and back, the final row move and the head's input: 4.

**Bit-exact by construction** — `float16_t(v)` on the same fp32 value the
move narrowed — and gated: `TestGraphHCLinkBitExact` runs a prefill and
one-, two- and three-row passes with the moves and with the link and
demands the same bits (100 → 28 moves over the five passes on the K-quant
bank, where the up rung is the GEMV; 100 → 60 on the Q8 bank, which has no
GEMV arm and links the output side alone). `LLM_HC_MOVES=1` /
`GraphOpts.HCMoves` keeps every move and is the control.

**Measured, same hour, three interleaved pairs** (`-gen -attrib -n 256`,
48 layers, one binary): moves 25.13 / 25.15 / 25.13 ms → link **24.83 /
24.83 / 24.81**, 39.79 → **40.28 / 40.28 / 40.31 tok/s** (`p22b_{moves,link}{A,B,C}.csv`).
`move` 196 → 4 dispatches, 0.530 → 0.031 ms. **But `hc.up` grew 13.3 →
14.9 µs a dispatch (+0.156 ms)** and `hc.cn` 2.4 → 2.7 (+0.03), so the
step gave back a third of the 0.5: the move had also been *zeroing the
consumer's pad rows*, contiguously, and the linked kernel did the same from
the sixteen lanes of one wave, 63 to 127 scattered two-byte stores a lane.

**The pad rows are not needed on the decode plan at all.** Every consumer
asked for them because its GEMM rungs have no bounds check — DeltaNet and
attention to their widest tile, the MoE to 64 — but at one to three rows
every rung that reads the A operand is a GEMV (`qkvGemv != GEMVOff`; the
router's split-K kernel and the expert GEMVs) that reads ROWS rows and
not one more. Each `InPort` now says so and reports the run itself as its
row block on that plan, so neither the move nor the linked kernel writes a
zero row at decode; the zeroing that remains (the `LLM_DECODE_GEMM=1` arm)
is done by the whole workgroup in runs of sixteen halves. The gates above
and `TestGraphIsAChunkSplit` on the shipped banks are unchanged to the
digit by it — no rung read those rows.

P22B_ROUND2

## What this sets up
'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new)
old='''4. **The moves** (P22, 0.54 ms): L6c's single arena.
5. **P20** stands on 1.23 steps for a two-row pass and a 23% break-even.'''

| [P13](p13-long-context-prefill.md) | **128k completes, and the attention kernel's key block was twice as wide as it should have been.** A 128 000-cell prefill **runs**, for the first time in this vertical, at **471.7 tok/s** — and the thing stopping it was never `DispatchMultiMarked`'s marks, it was that **P0's submit budget had no depth term in it**. Every measurement behind P0's `322 us a dispatch + 582 ns a dispatch-row` was taken from cell zero, so `batchFor(rows)` went on handing back the same 660 dispatches at 2048 rows whether the cache was empty or held 128 000 cells; at 64 000 those 660 already held the gfx ring for ~1.53 s of the 2 s watchdog while the budget believed it was spending 0.86, and at ~115 000 they cross it. So the chunker walks the recorded sequence and cuts where the *accumulated* prediction reaches the budget, charging each dispatch what its own label costs, and rescales itself against what the last submit actually measured — **upwards only**, because the affine constant is an order out at one row and a scale that learned from decode steps would hand the next prefill four times its budget. That is P11-7's 1.40x collected as a **rung** after P11-7 lost 1.18x trying to collect it as a branch, and it is the rule that file drew, applied: change the loop's granularity, not what happens inside it. It is **prefill's rung and not decode's** — with it on both, decode at 128k went 22.94 → 22.27, because a decode step costs one wave's serial walk (P8) and halving the block doubles the walk. **The refusal is the idea that looked best going in.** `llm_attn_blocks.comp` compacts the live key blocks into an ascending per-query-tile list so the kernel iterates the list instead of the axis — bit-identical, gated as an equality, deleting **83% of the visits** at 128 000 cells for 0.001 ms a token — and it is **1.00x at every depth**, and 1.05x *against* at the narrow rung where there are twice as many dead blocks to skip. Third instance of one rule, now the engine's rather than any kernel's: *latency and redundant reads that matter at decode do not matter at prefill, because prefill has occupancy* — 3072 single-wave workgroups against a decode step's 24. Two changes hold. **The attention kernel's row max ran on sixteen lanes of sixty-four**: `for (i = lane; i < BM; i += WAVE)` with BM 16 and WAVE 64, KTIL times a block, two barriers and a store around each pass, each active lane then walking TILE cells serially with a `selected()` bit test. The whole key block is now staged at once (`stage` holds QT\*KTIL tiles, 2 KB of LDS) and RCL = WAVE/BM lanes share a row, folded by a **clustered subgroup max** — **bit-identical**, because a max has no rounding and the cells scanned are the same ones in the same order, and the wave is converged where the op is issued. **1.16x on the kernel at 512 tokens** and **+1.6-1.8% of a prefill token from 8000 cells on**. And **a K-quant block's header is one sixteen-byte load, not four dwords**: Q4_K/Q5_K open every block with `d`, `dmin` and twelve packed scale bytes, so at BK 32 a lane was issuing eight scalar loads a K-step against the nibbles' four `uvec4`s — L5b-7's rule for the third time. Every block of both formats is 16-byte aligned (region, row and block all multiples of 16) and `MoEGPU.build` now says so rather than trusting it; with the nibble extracted in two ops instead of four it is **`moe.up` 12 118 → 11 755 µs at 2048 tokens (1.031x)** with **`moe.down` (IQ4_NL, untouched) flat as the control**. **And four refusals, which close most of P11's open list.** **Both of `hc.cn`'s named suspects cost nothing**: deleting the 256-way reduction tree outright measures **5331.5 µs against 5325.8** — the eight barriers four times a token are **free**, so the non-bit-exact rewrite queued behind them would have bought zero — and replacing the per-token `gamma` read with a constant measures **5332.9**, because it is the same 40 KB every token and the MALL serves it. Its 57% of copy bandwidth is now unexplained *and* out of hypotheses. **The block skip hoisted out of the loop is 1.00x at every depth**: at 64k a query tile walks ~2000 blocks and skips ~1480, each paying a **dependent** global read, and a cost model where a dead block is ~20% of a live one reproduces `attn.attn`'s 9.8-against-16.0 TFLOP/s exactly — so the whole key range was voted on up front in one coalesced pass with a subgroup ballot, no atomics and no per-block barrier, and it bought **nothing**. The reason is the **exact converse of P8**: a decode step dispatches 24 single-wave workgroups and nothing hides a serial walk, but a 2048-token prefill dispatches **3072**, so that latency is already covered — *latency that matters at decode does not matter at prefill, because prefill has occupancy*. It is still live for decode, where it was deliberately never built. **The selection mask loop is 3.5-8%**, not the rest of the gap. **The MoE's per-element affine is a floor**: gutting the whole scale path is 1.21x at 2048 tokens, P12-2 takes the loads and integer ops out of that, and what remains — an int→float convert, an FMA and an f16 convert on every weight — has no bit-exact cheaper form, since packed fp16 costs thirteen bits of mantissa and `v_cvt_pkrtz` rounds the wrong way. **The ubatch remains the largest number on the board**: 2048 → 8192 is 1.16x and the curve has not flattened, which is a memory budget rather than a kernel. |

| [P14](p14-prefill-at-depth.md) | **The gather, and 128k prefills past 900 tok/s — the target met.** A 128 000-cell prefill goes from P13's **563.6** to **826.0 tok/s at ubatch 2048** (1.47x, falloff from depth zero 0.50x → 0.72x) and to **946.1 at 8192**, with decode unmoved as the control. content.text:
P22b is done: the 196 per-step moves are gone from decode, and the step went from 25.13 to 24.42 ms, 39.8 to 41.0 tok/s, bit-exact.

**What changed.** The four moves a layer copied activations across block arenas. Instead of L6c's shared arena, the kernels on either side of each boundary now bind the other block's buffer at a new binding 11. The `cn`/`combine` kernels read a sublayer's output where it lies, and the decode `up` GEMV writes the next sublayer's fp16 input straight from the register holding the value. The graph passes ports through a new `HCLink`, with a pipeline built per foreign buffer on first use, the way the mover already did. Files: `shaders/llm_common.glsl`, the three hc shaders, `llm/gpu.go`, `llm/graph.go`, and the three blocks' `InPort` methods.

**The second finding.** The first A/B gave back a third of the saving because `hc.up` was zeroing the consumers' pad rows from one wave. Those rows turned out to be dead at decode: every consumer's rung is a GEMV that reads only the run's rows. Each input port now says so, and that alone made the control arm 0.22 ms faster, because the kernels after each move no longer ran behind a megabyte of zero write-back.

| arm | step ms (3 pairs) | tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| moves, old ports | 25.13 / 25.15 / 25.13 | 39.8 |
| link, old ports | 24.83 / 24.83 / 24.81 | 40.3 |
| moves, no pad rows | 24.91 / 24.89 / 24.97 | 40.1 |
| link, no pad rows | 24.42 / 24.39 / 24.43 | 41.0 |

**Verification.** New gate `TestGraphHCLinkBitExact` demands identical bits between the moves and the link over a prefill and 1-, 2- and 3-row passes, and passes on both dense banks. The 48-layer TestGraphLogits digits are identical in both arms. `LLM_HC_MOVES=1` keeps every move as the control. Tables are in `results/p22b_link_*.csv`, the write-up is Finding 6 of the P19 note, and TODO.md and the memory are updated.

**Two things to know.**
- Two test failures predate this change and fail identically with the moves kept: the decode-schedule subtests of TestGraphIsAChunkSplit on the default Q8 bank, and the batched-rows subtest of TestGraphImageDecode. They look like the earlier session's uncommitted work. I did not touch them.
- I briefly destroyed `llm/gpu.go` with a bad scripted edit and recovered it byte-for-byte from the interleaved copy. The recovery was confirmed by the build, the diff against HEAD and the gates.

Nothing is committed; the auto-committer owns main. Next on the list are the epilogue fusions, then P20. `dn.scan` is a bytes problem for P24, not a scheduling one.

content.text:
Where the 24.42 ms step stands now, from today's final linked arm:

| part | ms | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| weights at the bus | ~16.4 | 6.33 GB a token at 242 GB/s; the floor at this format |
| weight streams under the bus | ~3.5 | moe.up/down, dn.qkv, the head, hc.down, all at 175–215 GB/s |
| weightless dispatches | ~2.5 | dn.scan 0.63, moe.route 0.27, hc.cn 0.25, twenty small ones |
| host | ~1.0 | n-gram gather 0.61, argmax 0.16, record 0.10, hand-over |

The bytes alone would allow 38.2 tok/s and we are at 41.0, because the cache absorbs part of the streams. So the shape of what is left is clear: small items add up to maybe 2 ms, and only one lever has a multiple.

**Ranked by what it can return:**

- **P20, speculation.** The only multiple. A two-row verification pass costs 1.23 steps, so a free draft breaks even at 23% acceptance. The MTP head measured 65.6% on prose and costs 0.21 of a step. Prompt-lookup drafting costs nothing and is unbuilt. This is the route from 41 to the 50–60 range. The plan says observers first: acceptance on chat and code, then the two-row cost today, then build only what prices above 1.2x.
- **P24, fewer bytes.** About +0.6 tok/s per 0.1 GB shed. The fp16 DeltaNet state would roughly halve dn.scan's 0.63 ms, and narrower banks on the dense side follow the same rule. Gated on the downstream accuracy eval, because wikitext perplexity at +1.74% may no longer separate plans.
- **The rest of P22, epilogue fusions.** Of the 2.5 ms weightless, perhaps 0.5–0.8 is recoverable: the MoE's route, permute and combine as fewer dispatches, dn.norm folded into dn.conv, the split-K reduces folded into their consumers. Each is 1–2% and each needs a bit-identity gate like today's.
- **P23, the host gather.** 0.6 ms a token, 2.5%, and a deployment question: residency of the 28.8 GB n-gram table or of the rows a conversation reaches. The argmax at 0.16 ms could move to the GPU cheaply as well.
- **The streams under the bus.** ~3.5 ms against 242 GB/s, but the two obvious attacks are measured dead: hoisting loads on the big GEMVs (P21b) and on the MoE up loop. What remains is dispatch shape, and P21c took the part that had an idea.

What is not on the table: the clock. Decode runs at 97 W with the shader clock near 800 MHz because it is memory-bound, so there are no matrix clocks to buy, and a decode kernel pays about three times per instruction what the ISA suggests. Batched throughput has its own list in CONCURRENCY.md and is a different problem.

If the aim is single-stream speed, the recommendation is P20a–c next: three observers of a few minutes each that settle whether speculation is worth building, before any more 1% kernel work.

content.text:
Yes. Two tests in the llm suite fail, and both fail identically with my change switched off, so they predate this session's work.

- **TestGraphIsAChunkSplit, the three decode-schedule subtests.** On the suite's default banks (the Q8 dense bank, the checkpoint's own MoE formats) a 512-token prompt fed one, two or three tokens at a time diverges from the whole-prompt result by rms 0.137 on a scale of 18.6. That is a wrong answer, not rounding. On the shipped banks the 1- and 2-row subtests pass and only the 3-row one fails, at rms 2.2e-3 against a 1e-3 bar.
- **TestGraphImageDecode, the batched-rows subtest.** A batched row's logit differs from the same slot's solo step in the fifth digit, on the default banks:

```
step 0, slot 0: logit 0 is -1.6336796 batched and -1.6336946 solo
```

I confirmed both with `LLM_HC_MOVES=1`, which restores every move, and the numbers were the same to the digit. The 3-row shipped-bank failure was also unchanged by the pad-row change, which is what told me no rung was reading those rows.

I did not investigate the cause. The pattern points at the earlier session's uncommitted work in the same tree, since the P21c hoist of `moe.down` and the P22a shared-expert fold both touched the decode MoE kernels and the Q8_0 route is the one the shipped plan never runs. The rms 0.137 case is the one worth a look first, because it is a real breakage on a bank the tests default to. I recorded both in the memory note so the next session does not mistake them for its own.

content.text:
All three failures are explained and fixed, and the suite is green.

**1. TestGraphIsAChunkSplit, decode-schedule subtests (rms 0.137: a wrong answer).** A dispatch-order bug in the shared-expert fold from P22a. The routed down dispatch can carry the shared expert's down as its last tile, and that tile reads the swiglu rows the shared up writes. In the mixed case, up split and down folded, the shared up was recorded two dispatches after the routed down, so the tile read stale rows. Only the checkpoint's own formats take that path: a Q8_0 shared gate and up against Q4_K routed ones, a Q5_1 shared down against Q5_1 routed. The shipped plan folds the up and splits the down, and the fold's block test folded both, so neither saw it. Fix: `MoEGPU.graph` records the shared up before the routed down. TestMoEGPUSharedFold now has a mixed arm that agrees with the split at rms 4e-10 and asserts the order. The subtests pass at rms 5.7e-4, 7.5e-4 and 8.4e-4.

**2. TestGraphImageDecode, batched rows versus solo steps (a fifth-digit difference).** P19 put the head on its GEMV at one row only, so a three-slot batched step ran the GEMM head and rounded differently from three solo steps. The head now builds the GEMV per row count up to three and plans it there, like every other decode GEMV. TestGraphHeadDecodeGEMV gates the three-row pass against the GEMM at rms 7.7e-6 of the logits' max, and the batched gate is bit-identical again. Batched decode also gets the faster head kernel from this, unmeasured.

**3. The shipped-bank 3-row subtest (rms 2.2e-3 against a 1e-3 bar).** Not a kernel. The up GEMV's rows at two and three rows are the exact bits of one-row dispatches on the model's own weights, checked by a new TestHCGPUUpGemvRowsAgree. The schedule is what moves: with the up on the GEMM, swapping the down projection's split-K rung, a pure reassociation, takes the same subtest from 7.6e-4 to 2.3e-3, while the 2-row schedule stays near 6e-4 under every arm. One channel of one token's recurrence swings by 5e-2, which is a near-tie downstream, most likely in routing. The multi-row bar is now 5e-3 with the measurement in the test comment. The signatures it exists to catch are 0.137 and 1.785.

**Verification.** The graph, MoE, hc, move and prerecord tests pass on the default banks, TestGraphIsAChunkSplit passes in full on both bank configurations, and TestMoEGPUGraph's pinned dispatch order was updated to the new one. The write-up is a postscript in the P19 note, with TODO.md and the memory updated. Files changed: `llm/gpu_moe.go`, `llm/gpu_head.go`, four test files and the new test. Nothing is committed.
